1. Neurology. 2026 Nov 10;107(9):e218624. doi: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000218624. Epub
 2026 Oct 8.

Acute Imbalance Syndrome vs Acute Vestibular Syndrome: Clinical and 
Topographical Differentiation.

Möhwald K(1)(2), Hadzhikolev H(1)(2), Eberle L(1)(2), Jaufenthaler P(1)(2), 
Strupp M(1)(2), Jahn K(1)(3), Conrad J(4), Zwergal A(1)(2).

Author information:
(1)German Center for Vertigo and Balance Disorders, DSGZ, LMU University 
Hospital, LMU Medizin, LMU Munich, Germany.
(2)Department of Neurology, LMU University Hospital, LMU Medizin, LMU Munich, 
Germany.
(3)Department of Neurology, Schön Klinik Bad Aibling, Germany; and.
(4)Division for Neurodegenerative Diseases, Department of Neurology, University 
Medicine Mannheim, Germany.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Stroke is a major differential diagnosis in patients 
with acute vertigo/dizziness or imbalance. Current diagnostic algorithms such as 
head impulse test, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and test of skew are optimized for 
presentations with spontaneous nystagmus (SPN), traditionally called acute 
vestibular syndrome (AVS). However, in recent studies, a relevant proportion of 
patients with stroke-related vertigo/dizziness had no SPN, but rather postural 
or gait imbalance, a phenotype lately termed acute imbalance syndrome (AIS). We 
aimed to outline the pathoanatomical differences of stroke-related AIS vs AVS 
and its clinical implications.
METHODS: Patients with MRI-proven stroke-related acute vertigo/dizziness or 
imbalance were included in this emergency department (ED) cohort study at LMU 
Hospital prospectively. Vestibular, ocular motor, and postural signs were 
documented (including SPN presence/intensity by video oculography, postural 
imbalance by posturography). Patients were classified as suffering from AIS or 
AVS based on the presence of SPN. Stroke lesion distribution was depicted in 
Montreal Neurological Institute space and supplemented by structural 
disconnectome mapping from the lesion cores. Multivariate lesion symptom-mapping 
based on support-vector regression and disconnectome mapping was applied for SPN 
intensity and sway path as surrogate markers for AVS and AIS.
RESULTS: Of 75 patients (age: 65.7 ± 13.3 years, 40% female), 58.7% were 
diagnosed with AIS, 38.7% with AVS, and 2.7% with central positional vertigo. In 
AIS, the lesion core was located in the anterior cerebellar lobe and deep 
cerebellar nuclei (superior cerebellar artery/posterior inferior cerebellar 
artery territory) connecting to the bilateral pontomesencephalic tegmentum 
through the superior cerebellar peduncle. AVS stroke lesions were mostly located 
in the posterior cerebellar/flocculonodular lobe (posterior inferior cerebellar 
artery/anterior inferior cerebellar artery territory) and connected to the 
ipsilesional vestibular nucleus (VN) and bilateral medial longitudinal fascicle 
(MLF) through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. SPN intensity correlated with 
voxels in the cerebellar lobules VI-IX connecting to VN and MLF. Postural sway 
was associated with a small local cluster in the cerebellar Crus I.
DISCUSSION: AIS accounts for more than half of patients with stroke-related 
vertigo/dizziness or imbalance. AIS lesions were located in the anterior 
cerebellar lobe, disturbing cerebellar-pontomesencephalic networks for posture 
and gait control. AVS lesions affected the posterior cerebellar/flocculonodular 
lobe and associated vestibulo-ocular reflex networks. Recognition of both 
clinical phenotypes is essential to identify all strokes among patients with 
vertigo/dizziness in the emergency setting.
